sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Goroutines and channels are common Go interview topics because they reveal whether a candidate can reason about work that overlaps. The important skill is not memorizing `go` and `<-`; it is explaining ownership, blocking, completion, cancellation, and resource limits as one lifecycle.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **A goroutine is a runtime-managed unit of concurrent execution.** The Go runtime maps runnable goroutines onto operating-system threads. Goroutine stacks start small and grow, but every goroutine and the resources it retains still have a cost.
- **A channel is a typed communication and synchronization value.** `ch <- value` sends and `value := <-ch` receives. Channel operations can establish the ordering needed to observe work safely.
- **Capacity moves the wait point.** An unbuffered channel performs a direct handoff. A buffered channel temporarily owns up to `cap(ch)` queued values; sends still block when it is full and receives still block when it is empty.
- **Lifecycle stays explicit.** Starting, canceling, waiting, and closing are separate operations with separate owners.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Start and wait** — `go f()` starts independent execution; use a result receive or WaitGroup when completion must be observed.
- **Create and direct** — `make(chan T)` is unbuffered, `make(chan T, n)` has capacity `n`, and `chan<- T` / `<-chan T` narrow capabilities.
- **Predict blocking** — reason from nil, open, buffered, unbuffered, closed, empty, and full states.
- **Own close** — the sending side closes a finite stream after the final possible send; a coordinator handles multiple senders.
- **Consume streams** — range ends only after close and drain, not when an open channel is briefly empty.
- **Cancel alternatives** — select between useful communication and `ctx.Done()`; avoid busy polling with an unnecessary default.
- **Choose tools by role** — channels transfer, mutexes guard shared state, WaitGroups join tasks, and context signals cancellation or deadlines.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Early process exit** — starting a goroutine does not make `main` wait. Synchronize on a real result or completion event instead of sleeping.
- **Unsafe close ownership** — sending after close and closing twice panic. With multiple senders, wait for them and close from one coordinator.
- **Nil-channel wait** — send and receive on nil never become ready. This is usually missed initialization, though it can intentionally disable a select case.
- **Abandoned pipeline** — when a consumer returns early, an upstream send can remain blocked. Propagate cancellation to every stage.
- **Unbounded concurrency** — goroutines are relatively cheap, not free. Bound active work to the CPU, connection pool, service limit, and memory budget.

sections.title: One-minute recap
sections.body: > *"A goroutine is an independently executing function scheduled by the Go runtime over operating-system threads. A channel transfers typed values and also synchronizes the matching operations. An unbuffered channel is a direct handoff; a buffered channel is a bounded queue and still blocks at its limits. I make the owner of every goroutine, channel close, result, and cancellation signal explicit. I use channels for value flow, mutexes for shared state, WaitGroups for completion, and context for cancellation or deadlines."*
